entries.2c53ec0faedf6e49f9a98974c60be58208e3a496: <div sID="gen3517" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Deut.9" sID="Deut.9"/> <div eID="gen3517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3518" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3519" type="x-p"/> The design of Moses in this chapter is to convince the people of Israel of their utter unworthiness to receive from God those great favours that were now to be conferred upon them, writing this, as it were, in capital letters at the head of their charter, "Not for your sake, be it known unto you," <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.32">Ezek. xxxvi. 32</reference>. I. He assures them of victory over their enemies, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.1-Deut.9.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He cautions them not to attribute their successes to their own merit, but to God's justice, which was engaged against their enemies, and his faithfulness, which was engaged to their fathers, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.4-Deut.9.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. III. To make it evident that they had no reason to boast of their own righteousness, he mentions their faults, shows Israel their transgressions, and the house of Jacob their sins. In general, they had been all along a provoking people, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.7-Deut.9.24">ver. 7-24</reference>. In particular, 1. In the matter of the golden calf, the story of which he largely relates, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.8-Deut.9.21">ver. 8-21</reference>. 2. He mentions some other instances of their rebellion, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.22-Deut.9.23">ver. 22, 23</reference>. And, 3. Returns, at <reference osisRef="Deut.9.25">ver. 25</reference>, to speak of the intercession he had made for them at Horeb, to prevent their being ruined for the golden calf.
entries.fd6fa15659c101b5c410c95f4614e1d310053dca: <div eID="gen3519" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3518" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Victory Promised. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3520" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear, O Israel: Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> to pass over Jordan this day, to go in to possess nations greater and mightier than thyself, cities great and fenced up to heaven, <hi type="super">2</hi> A people great and tall, the children of the Anakims, whom thou knowest, and <hi type="italic">of whom</hi> thou hast heard <hi type="italic">say,</hi> Who can stand before the children of Anak! <hi type="super">3</hi> Understand therefore this day, that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God <hi type="italic">is</hi> he which goeth over before thee; <hi type="italic">as</hi> a consuming fire he shall destroy them, and he shall bring them down before thy face: so shalt thou drive them out, and destroy them quickly, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath said unto thee. <hi type="super">4</hi> Speak not thou in thine heart, after that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath cast them out from before thee, saying, For my righteousness the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath brought me in to possess this land: but for the wickedness of these nations the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> doth drive them out from before thee. 5 Not for thy righteousness, or for the uprightness of thine heart, dost thou go to possess their land: but for the wickedness of these nations the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God doth drive them out from before thee, and that he may perform the word which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sware unto thy fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. <hi type="super">6</hi> Understand therefore, that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee not this good land to possess it for thy righteousness; for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> a stiffnecked people. <div eID="gen3520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3521" type="x-p"/> The call to attention (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">Hear, O Israel,</hi> intimates that this was a new discourse, delivered at some distance of time after the former, probably the next sabbath day. <div eID="gen3521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3522" type="x-p"/> I. Moses represents to the people the formidable strength of the enemies which they were now to encounter, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.1">v. 1</reference>. The nations they were to dispossess were mightier than themselves, not a rude and undisciplined rout, like the natives of America, that were easily made a prey of. But, should they besiege them, they would find their cities well fortified, according as the art of fortification then was; should they engage them in the field, they would find the people great and tall, of whom common fame had reported that there was no standing before them, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.2">v. 2</reference>. This representation is much the same with that which the evil spies had made (<reference osisRef="Num.13.28">Num. xiii. 28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.13.33">33</reference>), but made with a very different intention: that was designed to drive them from God and to discourage their hope in him; this to drive them to God and to engage their hope in him, since no power less than that which is almighty could secure and prosper them. <div eID="gen3522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3523" type="x-p"/> II. He assures them of victory, by the presence of God with them, notwithstanding the strength of the enemy, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.3">v. 3</reference>. "Understand therefore what thou must trust to for success, and which way thou must look; it is the Lord thy God that goes before thee, not only as thy captain, or commander-in-chief, to give direction, but as a consuming fire, to do execution among them. Observe, He shall destroy them, and then thou shalt drive them out. Thou canst not drive them out, unless he destroy them and bring them down. But he will not destroy them and bring them down, unless thou set thyself in good earnest to drive them out." We must do our endeavour in dependence upon God's grace, and we shall have that grace if we do our endeavour. <div eID="gen3523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3524" type="x-p"/> III. He cautions them not to entertain the least thought of their own righteousness, as if that had procured them this favour at God's hand: "Say not. <hi type="italic">For my righteousness</hi> (either with regard to my good character or in recompence for any good service) <hi type="italic">the Lord hath brought me in to possess this land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.4">v. 4</reference>); never think it is for thy righteousness or the uprightness of thy heart, that it is in consideration either of thy good conversation or of thy good disposition," <reference osisRef="Deut.9.5">v. 5</reference>. And again (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.6">v. 6</reference>) it is insisted on, because it is hard to bring people from a conceit of their own merit, and yet very necessary that it be done: "<hi type="italic">Understand</hi> (know it, and believe it, and consider it) that <hi type="italic">the Lord thy God giveth thee not this land for thy righteousness.</hi> Hadst thou been to come to it upon that condition, thou wouldst have been for ever shut out of it, <hi type="italic">for thou art a stiff-necked people.</hi>" Note, Our gaining possession of the heavenly Canaan, as it must be attributed to God's power and not to our own might, so it must be ascribed to God's grace and not to our own merit: in Christ we have both righteousness and strength; in him therefore we must glory, and not in ourselves, or any sufficiency of our own. <div eID="gen3524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3525" type="x-p"/> IV. He intimates to them the true reasons why God would take this good land out of the hands of the Canaanites, and settle it upon Israel, and they are borrowed from his own honour, not from Israel's deserts. 1. He will be honoured in the destruction of idolaters; they are justly looked upon as haters of him, and therefore he will visit their iniquity upon them. It is <hi type="italic">for the wickedness of these nations</hi> that God <hi type="italic">drives them out,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.9.4">v. 4</reference>, and again, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.5">v. 5</reference>. All those whom God rejects are rejected for their own wickedness: but none of those whom he accepts are accepted for their own righteousness. 2. He will be honoured in the performance of his promise to those that are in covenant with him: God swore to the patriarchs, who loved him and left all to follow him, that he would give this land to their seed; and therefore he would <hi type="italic">keep that promised mercy for thousands of those that loved him and kept his commandments;</hi> he would not suffer his promise to fail. It was for their fathers' sakes that they were beloved, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.28">Rom. xi. 28</reference>. Thus boasting is for ever excluded. See <reference osisRef="Eph.1.9">Eph. i. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">11</reference>.
entries.e4e4cc7ade5670d517d27f6c6bdc5c1cb6985e25: <div eID="gen3525" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Cautions Against Self-Righteousness; Israel Reminded of Their Rebellions. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3526" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Remember, <hi type="italic">and</hi> forget not, how thou provokedst the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God to wrath in the wilderness: from the day that thou didst depart out of the land of Egypt, until ye came unto this place, ye have been rebellious against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">8</hi> Also in Horeb ye provoked the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to wrath, so that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was angry with you to have destroyed you. <hi type="super">9</hi> When I was gone up into the mount to receive the tables of stone, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the tables of the covenant which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> made with you, then I abode in the mount forty days and forty nights, I neither did eat bread nor drink water: <hi type="super">10</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> delivered unto me two tables of stone written with the finger of God; and on them <hi type="italic">was written</hi> according to all the words, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake with you in the mount out of the midst of the fire in the day of the assembly. <hi type="super">11</hi> And it came to pass at the end of forty days and forty nights, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> gave me the two tables of stone, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the tables of the covenant. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Arise, get thee down quickly from hence; for thy people which thou hast brought forth out of Egypt have corrupted <hi type="italic">themselves;</hi> they are quickly turned aside out of the way which I commanded them; they have made them a molten image. <hi type="super">13</hi> Furthermore the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto me, saying, I have seen this people, and, behold, it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a stiffnecked people: <hi type="super">14</hi> Let me alone, that I may destroy them, and blot out their name from under heaven: and I will make of thee a nation mightier and greater than they. <hi type="super">15</hi> So I turned and came down from the mount, and the mount burned with fire: and the two tables of the covenant <hi type="italic">were</hi> in my two hands. <hi type="super">16</hi> And I looked, and, behold, ye had sinned against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, <hi type="italic">and</hi> had made you a molten calf: ye had turned aside quickly out of the way which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had commanded you. <hi type="super">17</hi> And I took the two tables, and cast them out of my two hands, and brake them before your eyes. <hi type="super">18</hi> And I fell down before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , as at the first, forty days and forty nights: I did neither eat bread, nor drink water, because of all your sins which ye sinned, in doing wickedly in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to provoke him to anger. 19 For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure, wherewith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was wroth against you to destroy you. But the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hearkened unto me at that time also. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was very angry with Aaron to have destroyed him: and I prayed for Aaron also the same time. <hi type="super">21</hi> And I took your sin, the calf which ye had made, and burnt it with fire, and stamped it, <hi type="italic">and</hi> ground <hi type="italic">it</hi> very small, <hi type="italic">even</hi> until it was as small as dust: and I cast the dust thereof into the brook that descended out of the mount. <hi type="super">22</hi> And at Taberah, and at Massah, and at Kibroth-hattaavah, ye provoked the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to wrath. <hi type="super">23</hi> Likewise when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sent you from Kadesh-barnea, saying, Go up and possess the land which I have given you; then ye rebelled against the commandment of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, and ye believed him not, nor hearkened to his voice. <hi type="super">24</hi> Ye have been rebellious against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> from the day that I knew you. <hi type="super">25</hi> Thus I fell down before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> forty days and forty nights, as I fell down <hi type="italic">at the first;</hi> because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had said he would destroy you. <hi type="super">26</hi> I prayed therefore unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and said, O Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , destroy not thy people and thine inheritance, which thou hast redeemed through thy greatness, which thou hast brought forth out of Egypt with a mighty hand. <hi type="super">27</hi> Remember thy servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; look not unto the stubbornness of this people, nor to their wickedness, nor to their sin: <hi type="super">28</hi> Lest the land whence thou broughtest us out say, Because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was not able to bring them into the land which he promised them, and because he hated them, he hath brought them out to slay them in the wilderness. <hi type="super">29</hi> Yet they <hi type="italic">are</hi> thy people and thine inheritance, which thou broughtest out by thy mighty power and by thy stretched out arm. <div eID="gen3526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3527" type="x-p"/> That they might have no pretence to think that God brought them to Canaan <hi type="italic">for their righteousness,</hi> Moses here shows them what a miracle of mercy it was that they had not long ere this been destroyed in the wilderness: "<hi type="italic">Remember, and forget not, how thou provokedst the Lord thy God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.7">v. 7</reference>); so far from purchasing his favour, thou hast many a time laid thyself open to his displeasure." Their fathers' provocations are here charged upon them; for, if God had dealt with their fathers according to their deserts, this generation would never have been, much less would they have entered Canaan. We are apt to forget our provocations, especially when the smart of the rod is over, and have need to be often put in mind of them, that we may never entertain any conceit of our own righteousness. Paul argues from the guilt which all mankind is under to prove that we cannot be <hi type="italic">justified before God</hi> by our own works, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.19-Rom.3.20">Rom. iii. 19, 20</reference>. If our works condemn us, they will not justify us. Observe, 1. They had been a provoking people ever since they came out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.7">v. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Forty years long,</hi> from first to last, were God and Moses grieved with them. It is a very sad character Moses now at parting leaves of them: <hi type="italic">You have been rebellious since the day I knew you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.9.24">v. 24</reference>. No sooner were they formed into a people than there was a faction formed among them, which upon all occasions made head against God and his government. Though the Mosaic history records little more than the occurrences of the first and last year of the forty, yet it seems by this general account that the rest of the years were not much better, but one continued provocation. 2. Even in Horeb they made a calf and worshipped it, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.8">v. 8</reference>, &c. That was a sin so heinous, and by several aggravations made so exceedingly sinful, that they deserved upon all occasions to be upbraided with it. It was done in the very place where the law was given by which they were expressly forbidden to worship God by images, and while the mountain was yet burning before their eyes, and Moses had gone up to fetch them the law in writing. They <hi type="italic">turned aside quickly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.9.16">v. 16</reference>. 3. God was very angry with them for their sin. Let them not think that God overlooked what they did amiss, and gave them Canaan for what was good among them. No, God had determined to destroy them (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.8">v. 8</reference>), could easily have done it, and would have been no loser by it; he even desired Moses to let him alone that he might do it, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.13-Deut.9.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. By this it appeared how heinous their sin was, for God is never angry with any above what there is cause for, as men often are. Moses himself, though a friend and favourite, trembled at the revelation of God's wrath from heaven against their ungodliness and unrighteousness (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">I was afraid of the anger of the Lord,</hi> afraid perhaps not for them only, but for himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.120">Ps. cxix. 120</reference>. 4. They had by their sin broken covenant with God, and forfeited all the privileges of the covenant, which Moses signified to them by <hi type="italic">breaking the tables,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.9.17">v. 17</reference>. A bill of divorce was given them, and thenceforward they might justly have been abandoned for ever, so that their mouth was certainly stopped from pleading any righteousness of their own. God had, in effect, disowned them, when he said to Moses (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.12">v. 12</reference>), "They are thy people, they are none of mine, nor shall they be dealt with as mine." 5. Aaron himself fell under God's displeasure for it, though he was the saint of the Lord, and was only brought by surprise or terror to be confederate with them in the sin: <hi type="italic">The Lord was very angry with Aaron,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.9.20">v. 20</reference>. No man's place or character can shelter him from the wrath of God if he have <hi type="italic">fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness.</hi> Aaron, that should have made atonement for them if the iniquity could have been purged away by sacrifice and offering, did himself fall under the wrath of God: so little did they consider what they did when they drew him in. 6. It was with great difficulty and very long attendance that Moses himself prevailed to turn away the wrath of God, and prevent their utter ruin. He fasted and prayed full forty days and forty nights before he could obtain their pardon, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.18">v. 18</reference>. And some think twice forty days (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.25">v. 25</reference>), because it is said, <hi type="italic">as I fell down before,</hi> whereas his errand in the first forty was not of that nature. Others think it was but one forty, though twice mentioned (as also in <reference osisRef="Deut.10.10">ch. x. 10</reference>); but this was enough to make them sensible how great God's displeasure was against them, and what a narrow escape they had for their lives. And in this appears the greatness of God's anger against all mankind that no less a person than his Son, and no less a price than his own blood, would serve to turn it away. Moses here tells them the substance of his intercession for them. He was obliged to own their stubbornness, and their wickedness, and their sin, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.27">v. 27</reference>. Their character was bad indeed when he that appeared an advocate for them could not give them a good word, and had nothing else to say in their behalf but that God had done great things for them, which really did but aggravate their crime (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.26">v. 26</reference>),—that they were the posterity of good ancestors (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.27">v. 27</reference>), which might also have been turned upon him, as making the matter worse and not better,—and that the Egyptians would reproach God, if he should destroy them, as unable to perfect what he had wrought for them (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.28">v. 28</reference>), a plea which might easily enough have been answered: no matter what the Egyptians say, while the heavens declare God's righteousness; so that the saving of them from ruin at that time was owing purely to the mercy of God, and the importunity of Moses, and not to any merit of theirs, that could be offered so much as in mitigation of their offence. 7. To affect them the more with the destruction they were then at the brink of, he describes very particularly the destruction of the calf they had made, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.21">v. 21</reference>. He calls it their <hi type="italic">sin:</hi> perhaps not only because it had been the matter of their sin, but because the destroying of it was intended for a testimony against their sin, and an indication to them what the sinners themselves did deserve. Those that made it were like unto it, and would have had no wrong done them if they had been thus stamped to dust, and consumed, and scattered, and no remains of them left. It was infinite mercy that accepted the destruction of the idol instead of the destruction of the idolaters. 8. Even after this fair escape that they had, in many other instances they provoked the Lord again and again. He needed only to name the places, for they carried the memorials either of the sin or of the punishment in their names (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.22">v. 22</reference>): at <hi type="italic">Taberah, burning,</hi> where God set fire to them for their murmuring,—at <hi type="italic">Massah, the temptation,</hi> where they challenged almighty power to help them,—and at <hi type="italic">Kibroth-hattaavah, the graves of lusters,</hi> where the dainties they coveted were their poison; and, after these, their unbelief and distrust at Kadesh-barnea, of which he had already told them (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.1-Deut.1.46">ch. i.</reference>), and which he here mentions again (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.23">v. 23</reference>), would certainly have completed their ruin if they had been dealt with according to their own merits. <div eID="gen3527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3528" type="x-p"/> Now let them lay all this together, and it will appear that whatever favour God should hereafter show them, in subduing their enemies and putting them in possession of the land of Canaan, it was not for their righteousness. It is good for us often to remember against ourselves, with sorrow and shame, our former sins, and to review the records conscience keeps of them, that we may see how much we are indebted to free grace, and may humbly own that we never merited at God's hand any thing but wrath and the curse.  <chapter eID="Deut.9"/> <div eID="gen3528" type="x-p"/>

entries.0a7a22e0268d45ca8de27d61de38ceda91d98429: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1727"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.9.1-Deut.9.25">De 9:1-25</reference>. Moses Dissuades Them from the Opinion of Their Own Righteousness.</title> <div sID="gen2312" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1727"/><hi type="bold">1. this day--</hi>means this time. The Israelites had reached the confines of the promised land, but were obliged, to their great mortification, to return. But now they certainly were to enter it. No obstacle could prevent their possession; neither the fortified defenses of the towns, nor the resistance of the gigantic inhabitants of whom they had received from the spies so formidable a description.<div eID="gen2312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cities great and fenced up to heaven--</hi>Oriental cities generally cover a much greater space than those in Europe; for the houses often stand apart with gardens and fields intervening. They are almost all surrounded with walls built of burnt or sun-dried bricks, about forty feet in height. All classes in the East, but especially the nomad tribes, in their ignorance of engineering and artillery, would have abandoned in despair the idea of an assault on a walled town, which to-day would be demolished in a few hours. <div eID="gen2313" type="x-p"/>
entries.08ba8e42f0815fa4cddb80527bc78d226e68cb06: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1728"/><div sID="gen2314" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1728"/><hi type="bold">4-6. Speak not thou in thine heart, ... saying, For my righteousness the Lord hath brought me in to possess this land--</hi>Moses takes special care to guard his countrymen against the vanity of supposing that their own merits had procured them the distinguished privilege. The Canaanites were a hopelessly corrupt race, and deserved extermination; but history relates many remarkable instances in which God punished corrupt and guilty nations by the instrumentality of other people as bad as themselves. It was not for the sake of the Israelites, but for His own sake, for the promise made to their pious ancestors, and in furtherance of high and comprehensive purposes of good to the world, that God was about to give them a grant of Canaan. <hi type="bold">7. Remember, and forget not, how thou provokedst the Lord--</hi>To dislodge from their minds any presumptuous idea of their own righteousness, Moses rehearses their acts of disobedience and rebellion committed so frequently, and in circumstances of the most awful and impressive solemnity, that they had forfeited all claims to the favor of God. The candor and boldness with which he gave, and the patient submission with which the people bore, his recital of charges so discreditable to their national character, has often been appealed to as among the many evidences of the truth of this history. <div eID="gen2314" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d746f6545b8f40edfd80476ae7cde5e8c3d6861: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1729"/><div sID="gen2315" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1729"/><hi type="bold">8. Also in Horeb--</hi>rather, "even in Horeb," where it might have been expected they would have acted otherwise. <div eID="gen2315" type="x-p"/>
entries.84ea9e565463ffae9800ae235eb9825de6eb74bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1730"/><div sID="gen2316" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1730"/><hi type="bold">12-29. Arise, get thee down quickly from hence; for thy people ... have corrupted themselves--</hi>With a view to humble them effectually, Moses proceeds to particularize some of the most atrocious instances of their infidelity. He begins with the impiety of the golden calf--an impiety which, while their miraculous emancipation from Egypt, the most stupendous displays of the Divine Majesty that were exhibited on the adjoining mount, and the recent ratification of the covenant by which they engaged to act as the people of God, were fresh in memory, indicated a degree of inconstancy or debasement almost incredible. <div eID="gen2316" type="x-p"/>

entries.f4bdb312a7cca2b15629b9304db98cb2a5694f0e: <div eID="gen6634" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen6635" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6636" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6636" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6635" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6637" type="x-p"/> The people are informed that they shall shortly pass over Jordan, and that God shall go over before them, to expel the ancient inhabitants, <reference osisRef="Deu.9.1-Deu.9.3">Deu 9:1-3</reference>. They are cautioned not to suppose that it is on account of their righteousness that God is to give them that land, <reference osisRef="Deu.9.4-Deu.9.6">Deu 9:4-6</reference>. They are exhorted to remember their various provocations of the Divine Majesty, especially at Horeb, <reference osisRef="Deu.9.7-Deu.9.14">Deu 9:7-14</reference>; and how Moses interceded for them, and destroyed the golden calf, <reference osisRef="Deu.9.15-Deu.9.21">Deu 9:15-21</reference>. How they murmured at Taberah, <reference osisRef="Deu.9.22">Deu 9:22</reference>; and rebelled at Kadesh-barnea, <reference osisRef="Deu.9.23">Deu 9:23</reference>; and had been perverse from the beginning, <reference osisRef="Deu.9.24">Deu 9:24</reference>. An account of the intercession of Moses in their behalf, <reference osisRef="Deu.9.25-Deu.9.29">Deu 9:25-29</reference>. <div eID="gen6637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6638" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen6638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6639" type="x-p"/> Thou art to pass over Jordan this day - היום haiyom, this time; they had come thirty-eight years before this nearly to the verge of the promised land, but were not permitted at that day or time to pass over, because of their rebellions; but this time they shall certainly pass over. This was spoken about the eleventh month of the fortieth year of their journeying, and it was on the first month of the following year they passed over; and during this interim Moses died.
entries.f9ce82b603feaf0940b5a05a2c9fd71677c5d12f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen6639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6640" type="x-p"/> For the wickedness of these nations - So then it was not by any sovereign act of God that these people were cast out, but for their wickedness; they had transgressed the law of their Creator; they had resisted his Spirit, and could no longer be tolerated. The Israelites were to possess their land, not because they deserved it, but first, because they were less wicked than the others; and secondly, because God thus chose to begin the great work of his salvation among men. Thus then the Canaanites were cut off, and the Israelites were grafted in; and the Israelites, because of their wickedness, were afterwards cut off and the Gentiles grafted in. Let the latter not be high-minded, but fear; if God spared not the natural branches, take heed lest he spare not thee. But let it be remembered that this land was originally their own, and that the present possessors had no legal right to it.
entries.ed95a388cc3792dd41c5b64f022b14320284b4ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen6640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6641" type="x-p"/> Tables of stone - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Exo.31.18">Exo 31:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.32.15">Exo 32:15</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Exo.32.16">Exo 32:16</reference>.
entries.5e4f63ee5615722ef8bf73788102362fa7cddb36: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen6641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6642" type="x-p"/> Thy people - have corrupted themselves - Debased themselves by making and worshipping an Egyptian idol. See on Exodus 32 (note).
entries.befd9473890269eed9e8a336e0748647425c1459: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen6642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6643" type="x-p"/> I took your sin, the calf which ye had made - See this fully explained <reference osisRef="Exo.32.20">Exo 32:20</reference> (note).
entries.d729391bd747609f0bae9d9653e7e0dde96dc655: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen6643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6644" type="x-p"/> At Kibroth-hattaavah - See the note on <reference osisRef="Num.11.34">Num 11:34</reference>.
entries.68015fbb46e370c95e1479c25715b22a0843fd1b: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen6644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6645" type="x-p"/> Remember thy servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob - As if he had said: "These are their descendants, and the covenant was made with those patriarchs in behalf of these." God bestows many blessings on comparatively worthless persons, either for the sake of their pious ancestors, or on account of the religious people with whom they are connected; therefore union with the Church of God is a blessing of no common magnitude. The reader will find the grand subject of this chapter explained at large in the notes on Exodus 31 and 32, to which he is particularly desired to refer.  <chapter eID="Deut.9"/> <div eID="gen6645" type="x-p"/>

entries.6bd685ed539e012fe5c26d9fccda494c8db1b381: <div eID="gen2252" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Warning Against Self-Righteousness, Founded upon the Recital of Their Previous Sins - Deuteronomy 9-10:11</title> <div sID="gen2253" type="x-p"/> Besides the more vulgar pride which entirely forgets God, and attributes success and prosperity to its own power and exertion, there is one of a more refined character, which very easily spreads-namely, pride which acknowledges the blessings of God; but instead of receiving them gratefully, as unmerited gifts of the grace of the Lord, sees in them nothing but proofs of its own righteousness and virtue. Moses therefore warned the Israelites more particularly of this dangerous enemy of the soul, by first of all declaring without reserve, that the Lord was not about to give them Canaan because of their own righteousness, but that He would exterminate the Canaanites for their own wickedness (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.1-Deut.9.6">Deu 9:1-6</reference>); and then showing them for their humiliation, by proofs drawn from the immediate past, how they had brought upon themselves the anger of the Lord, by their apostasy and rebellion against their God, directly after the conclusion of the covenant at Sinai; and that in such a way, that it was only by his earnest intercession that he had been able to prevent the destruction of the people (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.7-Deut.9.24">Deut 9:7-24</reference>), and to secure a further renewal of the pledges of the covenant (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.25-Deut.10.11">Deut 9:25-10:11</reference>). <div eID="gen2253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2254" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Deut.9.1-Deut.9.3">Deu 9:1-3</reference> Warning against a conceit of righteousness, with the occasion for the warning. As the Israelites were now about to cross over the Jordan (“this day,” to indicate that the time was close at hand), to take possession of nations that were superior to them in size and strength (the tribes of Canaan mentioned in <reference osisRef="Deut.7.1">Deu 7:1</reference>), and great fortified cities reaching to the heavens (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.1.28">Deu 1:28</reference>), namely, the great and tall nation of the Enakites (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.28">Deu 1:28</reference>), before which, as was well known, no one could stand (התיצּב, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.7.24">Deu 7:24</reference>); and as they also knew that Jehovah their God was going before them to destroy and humble these nations, they were not to say in their heart, when this was done, For my righteousness Jehovah hath brought me in to possess this land. In <reference osisRef="Deut.9.3">Deu 9:3</reference>, היּום וידעתּ is not to be taken in an imperative sense, but as expressive of the actual fact, and corresponding to <reference osisRef="Deut.9.1">Deu 9:1</reference>, “thou art to pass.” Israel now knew for certain - namely, by the fact, which spoke so powerfully, of its having been successful against foes which it could never have conquered by itself, especially against Sihon and Og - that the Lord was going before it, as the leader and captain of His people (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>: see <reference osisRef="Deut.1.30">Deu 1:30</reference>). The threefold repetition of הוּא in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.3">Deu 9:3</reference> is peculiarly emphatic. “<hi type="italic">A consuming fire:</hi>” as in Deu 4:24. ישׁמידם הוּא is more particularly defined by וגו יכניעם והוּא, which follows: not, however, as implying that השׁמיד does not signify complete destruction in this passage, but rather as explaining how the destruction would take place. Jehovah would destroy the Canaanites, by bring them down, humbling them before Israel, so that they would be able to drive them out and destroy them quickly “מהר, quickly, is no more opposed to <reference osisRef="Deut.7.22">Deu 7:22</reference>, 'thou mayest not destroy them quickly,' than God’s not delaying to requite (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.10">Deu 7:10</reference>) is opposed to His long-suffering” (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>). So far as the almighty assistance of God was concerned, the Israelites would quickly overthrow the Canaanites; but for the sake of the well-being of Israel, the destruction would only take place by degrees. “<hi type="italic">As Jehovah hath said unto thee:</hi>” viz., <reference osisRef="Exod.23.23">Exo 23:23</reference>, Exo 23:27., and at the beginning of the conflict, Deu 2:24.
entries.04b1d80ae45b91978d34f93bc83f9623eca12630: <reference osisRef="Deut.9.4-Deut.9.6">Deu 9:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen2254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2255" type="x-p"/> When therefore Jehovah thrust out these nations before them (הדף, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.6.19">Deu 6:19</reference>), the Israelites were not to say within themselves, “<hi type="italic">By</hi> (for, on account of) <hi type="italic">my righteousness Jehovah hath brought me</hi> (led me hither) <hi type="italic">to possess this land</hi>.” The following word, וּברשׁעת, is adversative: “<hi type="italic">but because of the wickedness of these nations</hi>,” etc. - To impress this truth deeply upon the people, Moses repeats the thought once more in Deu 9:5. At the same time he mentions, in addition to righteousness, straightness or uprightness of heart, to indicate briefly that outward works do not constitute true righteousness, but that an upright state of heart is indispensable, and then enters more fully into the positive reasons. The wickedness of the Canaanites was no doubt a sufficient reason for destroying <hi type="italic">them</hi>, but not for giving their land to the people of Israel, since they could lay no claim to it on account of their own righteousness. The reason for giving Canaan to the Israelites was simply the promise of God, the word which the Lord had spoken to the patriarchs on oath (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.7.8">Deu 7:8</reference>), and therefore nothing but the free grace of God, - not any merit on the part of the Israelites who were then living, for they were a people “of a hard neck,” i.e., a stubborn, untractable generation. With these words, which the Lord Himself had applied to Israel in <reference osisRef="Exod.32.9">Exo 32:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.33.3">Exo 33:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.33.5">Exo 33:5</reference>, Moses prepares the way for passing to the reasons for his warning against self-righteous pride, namely, the grievous sins of the Israelites against the Lord.
entries.c62a94e9922d9dc77e3e77e13c1ed1638f3a992d: <reference osisRef="Deut.9.7-Deut.9.24">Deu 9:7-24</reference> <div eID="gen2255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2256" type="x-p"/> He reminded the people how they had provoked the Lord in the desert, and had shown themselves rebellious against God, from the day of their departure from Egypt till their arrival in the steppes of Moab. את־אשׁר, for אשׁר, is the object to תּשׁכּח (<hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §333, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.): “<hi type="italic">how</hi> thou hast provoked.” המרה, generally with את־פּי (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.1.26">Deu 1:26</reference>), to be rebellious against the commandment of the Lord: here with עם, construed with a person, to deal rebelliously <hi type="italic">with</hi> God, to act rebelliously in relation to Him (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.31.27">Deu 31:27</reference>). The words “<hi type="italic">from the day that thou camest out</hi>,” etc., are not to be pressed. It is to be observed, however, that the rebellion against the guidance of God commenced before they passed through the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.11">Exo 14:11</reference>). This general statement Moses then followed up with facts, first of all describing the worship of the calf at Horeb, according to its leading features (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.8-Deut.9.21">Deu 9:8-21</reference>), and then briefly pointing to the other rebellions of the people in the desert (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.22">Deu 9:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.23">Deu 9:23</reference>).
entries.b4bc19870ed0cd428cb4f83d928bed07829fe46a: <reference osisRef="Deut.9.25-Deut.9.29">Deu 9:25-29</reference> <div eID="gen2260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2261" type="x-p"/> After vindicating in this way the thought expressed in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.7">Deu 9:7</reference>, by enumerating the principal rebellions of the people against their God, Moses returns in Deu 9:25. to the apostasy at Sinai, for the purpose of showing still further how Israel had no righteousness or ground for boasting before God, and owed its preservation, with all the saving blessings of the covenant, solely to the mercy of God and His covenant faithfulness. To this end he repeats in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.26-Deut.9.29">Deu 9:26-29</reference> the essential points in his intercession for the people after their sin at Sinai, and then proceeds to explain still further, in <reference osisRef="Deut.10.1-Deut.10.11">Deu 10:1-11</reference>, how the Lord had not only renewed the tables of the covenant in consequence of this intercession (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.1-Deut.10.5">Deu 10:1-5</reference>), but had also established the gracious institution of the priesthood for the time to come by appointing Eleazar in Aaron’s stead as soon as his father died, and setting apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the covenant and attend to the holy service, and had commanded them to continue their march to Canaan, and take possession of the land promised to the fathers (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.6-Deut.10.11">Deu 10:6-11</reference>). With the words “thus I fell down,” in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.25">Deu 9:25</reference>, Moses returns to the intercession already briefly mentioned in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.18">Deu 9:18</reference>, and recalls to the recollection of the people the essential features of his plea at the time. For the words “<hi type="italic">the forty days and nights that I fell down</hi>,” see at Deu 1:46. The substance of the intercession in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.26-Deut.9.29">Deu 9:26-29</reference> is essentially the same as that in <reference osisRef="Exod.32.11-Exod.32.13">Exo 32:11-13</reference>; but given with such freedom as any other than Moses would hardly have allowed himself (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>), and in such a manner as to bring it into the most obvious relation to the words of God in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.12">Deu 9:12</reference>, Deu 9:13. אל־תּשׁחת, “<hi type="italic">Destroy not Thy people and Thine inheritance</hi>,” says Moses, with reference to the words of the Lord to him: “<hi type="italic">thy people have corrupted themselves</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.12">Deu 9:12</reference>). Israel was not Moses’ nation, but the nation and inheritance of Jehovah; it was not Moses, but Jehovah, who had brought it out of Egypt. True, the people were stiffnecked (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.9.13">Deu 9:13</reference>); but let the Lord remember the fathers, the oath given to Abraham, which is expressly mentioned in <reference osisRef="Exod.32.13">Exo 32:13</reference> (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.7.8">Deu 7:8</reference>), and not turn to the stiffneckedness of the people (קשׁי equivalent to ערף קשׁה, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.13">Deu 9:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.9.6">Deu 9:6</reference>), and to their wickedness and sin (i.e., not regard them and punish them). The honour of the Lord before the nations was concerned in this (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.28">Deu 9:28</reference>). The land whence Israel came out (“the land” = the people of the land, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.10.25">Gen 10:25</reference>, etc., viz., the Egyptians: the word is construed as a collective with a plural verb) must not have occasion to say, that Jehovah had not led His people into the promised land from incapacity or hatred. יכלת מבּלי recalls Num 14:16. Just as “inability” would be opposed to the nature of the absolute God, so “hatred” would be opposed to the choice of Israel as the inheritance of Jehovah, which He had brought out of Egypt by His divine and almighty power (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.6.6">Exo 6:6</reference>).  <chapter eID="Deut.9"/> <div eID="gen2261" type="x-p"/>

entries.dfd9bff33e6bf416422c68ba8aaed701c176cdc5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.9.1" sID="gen8684" type="section"/> <div sID="gen8685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">Thou art to pass over Jordan this day.</hi> The whole of this passage contains an eulogy on the gratuitous liberality of God, whereby He had bound the people to Himself unto the obedience of the Law. But this (as we have already seen) ought to have been a most pressing stimulus to incite the people, and altogether to ravish them to the worship and love of God, to whom they were under so great obligation. The design of Moses, then, was to shew that the Israelites, for no merit of their own, but by the signal bounty of God, would be heirs of the land of Canaan; and that this entirely flowed from the covenant and their gratuitous adoption; in order that, on their part, they should persevere in the faithful observation of the covenant, and so should be the more disposed to honor Him. For it would be too disgraceful that they, whom God had prevented by His grace, should not meet Him, as it were, by voluntarily submitting to His dominion. Moreover, lest they should arrogate anything to themselves, he commends the greatness of God’s power, in that they could not be victorious over so many nations, unless by the miraculous aid of heaven. With this view, he states that these nations excelled not only in greatness and multitude, but also in military valor. He adds that their cities were great and impregnable; and, finally, that in them were the children of the giants, formidable from their enormous stature. For Anak (as is related in <reference osisRef="Bible:Josh.15">Joshua 15</reference><note n="246"> <div sID="gen8686" type="x-p"/> Or, more fully in <reference osisRef="Bible:Num.13.33">Numbers 13:33</reference>.<div eID="gen8686" type="x-p"/> </note> ) was a celebrated giant, whose descendants were called Anakim. And, to take away all doubt about this, he cites themselves as witnesses, that they were so terrified by their appearance as to wish to turn back again. We now understand the object of all these details, viz., that God’s glory may shine forth in the victories and success of the people. The words “whom thou knowest, and of whom thou hast heard,” have reference to the spies;<note n="247"> <div sID="gen8687" type="x-p"/> “Qui avoyent este envoyez pour descouvrir la terre;” who had been sent to descry the land. — <hi type="italic">Fr.</hi><div eID="gen8687" type="x-p"/> </note> for these giants had not yet become openly known to the people; but he transfers the case of a few to them all, because, by the account the spies had given, terror had invaded the whole camp, as though they had actually come into conflict with them. Since, then, they had been persuaded of their inferiority to their enemies, and utterly disheartened by the report they received, Moses convicts them on their own evidence, lest, perchance, they might hereafter assume to themselves the praise which was due to God alone. But we are taught in these words, that such is the ingratitude of mankind, that they obscure, as much as they can, God’s bounties, and never yield, except when driven to conviction.<div eID="gen8685" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen8684" osisID="Deut.9.1" type="section"/>
entries.7bfd13f376c87d7c88b8eb5a9f460cf20ffb5736: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.9.3" sID="gen8688" type="section"/> <div sID="gen8689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">Understand therefore this day.</hi> He concludes from what has preceded that the Israelites would be too perverse, unless they acknowledge that their enemies were overcome by the hand of God; and, still more to heighten the miracle, he uses a similitude, comparing God to a fire, which consumes so many nations in an unwonted and incredible manner. It is as if he had said, that it could not be effected by human or ordinary means that so many and such warlike peoples could thus quickly perish. Elsewhere God is called “a consuming fire” in a different sense, that we may fear his wrath and power; but here Moses only means that the destruction of the Canaanitish nations was His wonderful work.<div eID="gen8689" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen8688" osisID="Deut.9.3" type="section"/>
entries.081b73b215bb1ee55df9e137382e4a5d2ee71dab: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.9.4" sID="gen8690" type="section"/> <div sID="gen8691" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi> <hi type="italic">Speak not thou in thine heart.</hi> He now more plainly warns the people not to exalt themselves in proud and foolish boasting. If they had not been naturally so depraved and malignant, it would have been sufficient to point out God’s grace in a single word; but he could not induce them to gratitude except by correcting and destroying their pride. He therefore takes away this stumblingblock, in order that God’s generosity might be conspicuous among them. “To speak in the heart” is equivalent to reflecting or conceiving an opinion. Wherefore Moses not only reproves the boasting of the lips, but that hidden arrogance, wherewith men are puffed up, when they take to themselves the praise which is due to God. Moreover, he not only prohibits them from ascribing it to their own valor, that they had routed their enemies, and gained possession of the land, but also from imagining that this was the just recompense of their merits. For God is not less defrauded of His glory when men oppose their righteousness to His liberality, than when they boast that whatever blessings they have are obtained by their own industry. To make this more ‘clear, I will repeat it. Moses does not forbid the people from thinking that they had themselves acquired the land without God’s aid; nay, he takes it for granted that they themselves will acknowledge that it was by God’s help that they were victorious; but he is not contented with this limited gratitude unless they at the same time acknowledge that they had deserved nothing of the kind, and therefore that it was a mere and gratuitous act of His bounty. The reason given in the second clause does not appear sufficiently<note n="248"> <div sID="gen8692" type="x-p"/> De prime face. — <hi type="italic">Fr.</hi><div eID="gen8692" type="x-p"/> </note> conclusive, viz., that the nations were driven out on account of their own wickedness; for it might have been that what God took away from these wicked reprobates He transferred to those who were more worthy; but. it appears to be an indirect admonition, that the Israelites should compare themselves with these nations; because it was evidently to be gathered by them from thence,<note n="249"> <div sID="gen8693" type="x-p"/> “Pour ce que, se cognoissans povres et miserables, ils devoyent aisement conclurre,” etc.; because, knowing themselves to be poor and miserable, they might easily conclude, etc. —<hi type="italic"> Fr.</hi><div eID="gen8693" type="x-p"/> </note> that they had not acquired this foreign land, from which the former inhabitants had been ejected, by their own righteousness. And this is still more clearly expressed in the two next verses.<div eID="gen8691" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen8690" osisID="Deut.9.4" type="section"/>

5. Not for thy righteousness. First of all, he would have the punishment inflicted upon these nations awaken the Israelites to fear, and thus that they should attribute nothing to themselves; because it was God’s design not to reward their merits, but to shew the severity of His judgment. Secondly, he confirms this by two arguments; viz., because God thus had performed what He promised Abraham; (which promise, as has been already seen, was founded on mere grace;) and, again, because the people itself was naturally perverse and rebellious. Hence, it sufficiently appears that there was no room for merits, since by them God’s covenant would have been nullified, nor, if there were, could any such be found in so depraved and contumacious a nation. And besides, God had made His covenant with Abraham almost four centuries before they were born. Hence it follows that this benefit proceeded from some other source. But he still further represses their pride, by reproaching them with being “stiff-necked;” for it would have been too absurd to imagine that God, whom they had not ceased to provoke with their sins, was under obligation to them, as if they had duly discharged their duty. This metaphor is taken from oxen, which are useless until they are accustomed to bend their necks; it is then the same as saying that they were not only unsubmissive, but that in their obstinacy they shook off the yoke. By his impressing on them, for the third time, that the Israelites had not deserved the land by their righteousness, we learn that nothing is more difficult than for men to strip themselves of their blind arrogance, whereby they detract some portion of the praise from God’s mercies. Now, if in regard to an earthly inheritance God so greatly exalts His mercy, what must we think of the heavenly inheritance?
L’heritage celeste, et permanent. — Fr.
He would have it attributed to Himself alone, that the children of Israel possess the land of Canaan; how much less, then, will He tolerate the obtrusion of men’s merits in order to the acquisition of heaven? Nor is there anything in the pretense of the Papists that they attribute the first place to God’s bounty; because He claims altogether for Himself what they would share with Him. But if any object that this was only said to His ancient people, I reply, that we are no better than they. Let each retire into himself,
Pour se bien examiner. — Fr.
and he will not excuse the hardness of his neck. But they who are regenerated by God’s Spirit, know that they are not naturally formed unto obedience; and thus that it is only mercy which makes them to differ from the worst of men.
DEUTERONOMY 10
Deuteronomy 10:21, 22
21. He is thy praise, and he is thy God, that hath done for thee these great and terrible things which thine eyes have seen.
21. Jehova est laus tua, et ipse est Dens qui fecit tecum magna et terribilia ista quae viderunt oculi tui.

entries.1722e373a4ea0588add67301c25dfbc0737f13a3: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.9.7" sID="gen17844" type="section"/><p/> <div sID="gen17845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7. </hi><hi type="italic">Remember, and forget not, how thou provokedst</hi> In order to reprove the ingratitude of the people, Moses here briefly refers to some of their offenses; but he principally insists on the history of their revolt, in which their extreme and most detestable impiety betrayed itself. He therefore narrates this crime in almost the identical words which he had previously used in Exodus. He begins by urging them often to reflect upon their sins, lest they should ever be forgotten; and this constant recollection of them not only tended to humiliate them, but also to teach them at length to lay aside their depraved nature, and to accustom themselves to become obedient to God. Afterwards he proceeds to the history itself, shewing that God had been provoked by their idolatry to destroy them. If a question be here put, how it was that God was prevailed upon by Moses to change His intention, our curiosity must be repressed, lest we should dispute more deeply than is fitting respecting the secret and incomprehensible decree of God. Sure it is that God did not act otherwise than He had determined; but Moses goes no deeper than the sentence that was revealed to him; just as we must assuredly conclude that destruction is prepared for us when we transgress; and that God’s anger is appeased when we fly to His mercy in true faith, and with sincere affections. The rest has been already expounded.<div eID="gen17845" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen17844" osisID="Deut.9.7" type="section"/>
entries.6f0d1770a89c20ecdff1a92465f4a64cdafd9d2a: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.9.17" sID="gen17846" type="section"/> <div sID="gen17847" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17. </hi><hi type="italic">And I took the two tables, and cast them out</hi> Moses here accuses himself of no transgression; he does not, therefore, give us to understand that he was urged to break the tables by the impetuosity of excessive anger; but rather he again repeats what they had deserved, and consequently that he discharged the office of a herald, <note n="391"> <div sID="gen17848" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lat.</hi> “Fecialis munere;” alluding doubtless to the custom of the Roman <hi type="italic">Feciales,</hi> in throwing a bloody spear into the territories of others as a declaration of war. See <hi type="italic">Liv.</hi> 1:32.<div eID="gen17848" type="x-p"/> </note> so as to denounce, not by word of mouth only, but by a solemn rite also, that God’s Covenant was broken and made void by their perfidiousness. For which reason also he cast down and broke the tables before their eyes, in order that being alarmed by so awful a punishment, they might more earnestly betake themselves to the expiation of their sins.<div eID="gen17847" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen17846" osisID="Deut.9.17" type="section"/>
entries.64d2bc64f610123ee8536e6216247c3e7f5d2808: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.18" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.9.18" sID="gen17849" type="section"/> <div sID="gen17850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18. </hi><hi type="italic">And I fell down before the Lord</hi> The order of the narrative is confused; for this fact of which he speaks did not precede his second ascent into the mount, when he was commanded to prepare the second tables. If so, he would have fasted three times, which we gather from other passages not to have been the case; but we must not be surprised that the same thing should be often repeated, as we shall see at the beginning of chapter 10, as well as shortly afterwards. The mention of it here, however, is seasonable, because the Covenant was to be renewed, and therefore, as if nothing had been done, he again abstained from meat and drink for forty days. Yet we have elsewhere seen that there were other prayers which had intervened before He ascended the mount a second time; but He does not here distinctly record the details, nay, he mixes up the prayers, whereby he interceded with God, with the second fast, because this was the point most worthy of observation, that the first promulgation of the Law had failed of its effect, and the Covenant which they had violated was to be repeated, as it were, from its very commencement.<div eID="gen17850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17851" type="x-p"/>Although he says that “because of their sins” he had not eaten bread nor drunk water, he does not signify that this fast was a sign of grief and mourning, like as Joel invites the people to sackcloth and ashes, and urges them to weeping and fasting for the purpose of testifying their repentance. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Joel.2.12">Joel 2:12</reference>.) For abstinence, as I have already shewn, was no more difficult or grievous to Moses than to the angels. But he simply reminds them that so great a sin could not be expiated, unless he had again renounced the life of men and had been taken up to God. Meanwhile, it must be borne in mind that previously to this, he had already made entreaty for the people, and had also been accepted; inasmuch as it was a token that God was reconciled and appeased, when He called up Moses to receive the Law, and to bring it down to them a second time. To this refers what he adds in the next verse, “For I was afraid of the anger,” etc., for he was still in anxiety as to the welfare of the people, since God did not cease to menace them. We see, therefore, that this fear and anxious earnestness in prayer are separated from the fast, as different things; and assuredly he had already propitiated God, when, by His command he hewed out the new tables whereon the Covenant was to be renewed. Still, I do not deny that he labored also in the mount in the cause of obtaining pardon, just as believers, by continuing the requests which have already been granted, confirm their faith more and more. I only warn my readers to observe the distinction of time which I have noticed.<div eID="gen17851" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.18" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen17849" osisID="Deut.9.18" type="section"/>
entries.e674c7525d0cbb674d028d610f0c747610a25d75: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.9.20" sID="gen17852" type="section"/> <div sID="gen17853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20. </hi><hi type="italic">And the Lord was very angry with Aaron</hi> It hence appears how vain are the pretexts whereby men endeavor to conceal their faults, until they are subdued by genuine fear of God to acknowledge their guilt. Although Aaron did not boast that he was altogether innocent, still he endeavored to blot out, or at any rate to extenuate the enormity of his crime by alleging that he was under compulsion. But Moses declares that God was very angry with him. Whence it follows that he was guilty of a very gross sin, which is also more certainly declared by the greatness of its punishment; for God would never have been thus moved even to destroy him, unless because he was worthy of this condemnation.<div eID="gen17853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17854" type="x-p"/>In the next verse, the word <hi type="italic">sin</hi> is not applied to the act; itself, <note n="392"> <div sID="gen17855" type="x-p"/> “Il appelle le veau Peche du <hi type="italic">peuple,</hi> pource qu’il avoit este la matiere et object de leur idolatrie;” he calls the calf the Sin of the people, because it had been the matter and object of their idolatry. — <hi type="italic">Fr.</hi><div eID="gen17855" type="x-p"/> </note> but is transferred by metonymy to the calf, as its apposition shews. Again, by saying that he had thoroughly broken the calf to pieces by grinding it till it was reduced to powder, he signifies once more how abominable this idol was, especially when he adds, that the powder was cast into the stream, lest any memorial of it should continue in existence.<div eID="gen17854" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.9.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen17852" osisID="Deut.9.20" type="section"/>

Thus I fell down before the Lord forty days Again the narrative is blended together; for it is certain that this prayer was offered before he remained fasting in the mount during the second forty days. But inasmuch as then also, being still in anxiety, he continued the same prayers, it is not to be wondered at that he should include in the forty days’ fast whatever had been done before. For there is no absurdity in supposing that after having obtained the safety of the people, for which he had petitioned, he should still be in trepidation.                   <ns0:p n="16">16 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 32. 19.</ns0:note> I looked, and behold, ye had sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned against the LORD your God, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> had made you a molten calf: ye had turned aside quickly out of the way which the LORD had commanded you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And I took the two tables, and cast them out of my two hands, and brake them before your eyes <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Not by an unbridled passion, but in zeal for Gods honour, and by the direction of Gods spirit, to signifie to the people, that the covenant between God and them contained in those tables was broken and made void, and they were now quite cast out of Gods favour, and could expect nothing from him but fiery indignation and severe justice. See on <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 32. 19.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psa. 106. 23.</ns0:note> I fell down <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">In way of humiliation and supplication, on your behalf.</ns0:note> before the LORD, as at the first, forty dayes, and forty nights; I did nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther eat bread, nor drink water, because of all your sins, which ye sinned, in doing wickedly in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 (For I was afraid of the anger and hot dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pleasure wherewith the LORD was wroth against you, to destroy you) But the LORD hearkned un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to me at that time also.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And the LORD was very angry with Aaron <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Though he was onely accessary, as being perswaded, and in a manner compelled to comply with your desire.</ns0:note>, to have destroyed him: And I prayed for Aaron also the same time.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 32. 20.</ns0:note> I took your sin <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) The object and matter of your sin, as <ns0:hi>sin</ns0:hi> is taken <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 31. 7.</ns0:note>, the calf which ye had made, and burnt it with fire, and stamped it, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> ground <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> very small, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> until it was as small as dust: and I cast the dust thereof into the brook <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">That there might be no monument or remem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brance of it left.</ns0:note> that descended out of the mount.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And at <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Num. 11. 1, 3.</ns0:note> Taberah, and at <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 17. 7.</ns0:note> Massa, and at <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Num. 11. 34.</ns0:note> Kibroth-hattaavah, ye provoked the LORD to wrath.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 Likewise <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Num. 13. 3.</ns0:note> when the LORD sent you from Kadesh-barnea, saying, Go up, and possess the land which I have given you, then ye rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God, and ye believed him not, nor hearkned to his voice.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 Ye have been rebellious against the LORD, from the day that I knew you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 Thus I fell down before the LORD forty dayes, and forty nights <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">The same mentioned before <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 18. as appears, 1. By comparing this with <ns0:hi>Exodus,</ns0:hi> where this History is more fully re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lated, and where this is said to be done twice onely. 2. By the occasion and matter of <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> his prayer here following, which is the same with the former. 3. By the words here fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowing, <ns0:hi>as I fell down at first,</ns0:hi> which shew that this was the se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cond time of his so doing.</ns0:note>, as I fell down <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 18.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>at the first,</ns0:hi> because the LORD had said, he would de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroy you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 I prayed therefore unto the LORD and said, O LORD God, destroy not thy people, and thine inheritance, which thou hast redeemed through thy greatness <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Through the greatness of thy power, which ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />peared most eminently in that work, as is noted <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 29.</ns0:note>, which thou hast brought forth out of Egypt, with a mighty hand.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 Remember thy servants <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) The promise made and sworn to thy servants, which was mentioned above <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5.</ns0:note>, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: look not unto the stubborness of this people, nor to their wickedness, nor to their sin:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 Lest the land whence thou broughtest us out, say, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Num. 14. 15.</ns0:note> Because the LORD was not able to bring them into the land which he promised them, and because he hated them, he hath brought them out to slay them in the wilderness.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 Yet they <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> thy people <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Whom thou hast chosen to thy self out of all mankind, and publickly owned them for thine, and hast purchased and redeemed them from the <ns0:hi>Egyptians.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and thine inheri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tance, which thou broughtest out by thy mighty power, and by thy stretched-out arm.</ns0:p>
